exercise.name: Medicine Ball Seated Calf Raise
aliases: Seated calf raise with a medicine ball

reference.title: Medicine Ball Seated Calf Raise

reference.note: Reference used only to identify the movement. No GymVisual media is stored here; this rig, model and animation are original.

breathing.pattern: Exhale as the heels rise, inhale as they lower.
breathing.cadence: About 1 s up, 0.8 s pause, 1.8 s down

prescription.load: Ball weight is user-chosen (a 5-10 kg medicine ball is typical); go heavier or add reps when every rep reaches full height.
prescription.progression: Heavier dumbbells, then balls of the feet on a plate or step for a deeper stretch, then single-leg

cues.text: Sit on the end of the bench, feet flat a little wider than the hips, shins vertical; rest a medicine ball on the lower thighs just behind the knees and hold it there with a hand on each side.
Breathe out and press through the balls of the feet, lifting the heels and the ball as high as you can.
Pause at the top; weight over the big and second toes, ankles straight (no rolling out).
Breathe in and lower the heels slowly to the floor.
Touch down without bouncing and repeat.

mistakes.fix: Full range: heels all the way down, pause at the top, slow lowering.

mistakes.mistake: Feet rolling out onto the little toes
mistakes.fix: Keep the pressure on the big and second toes.

mistakes.mistake: Pushing the ball up with the arms
mistakes.fix: The hands only hold the ball in place; the calves lift it.
Shins vertical, knees over the ankles, so the load sits over the balls of the feet.

kinematics.norm: Full range from heels down to as high as possible; the seated knee-90 position biases the soleus (Kinoshita 2023)
Lift as high as possible each rep (clinical opinion)
About 90 degrees, as in the seated training condition of Kinoshita 2023; the knee rises with the heel

kinematics.setup: 30 cm ball on the lower thighs, centre 6 cm behind the knees, palms on its sides
kinematics.peak: Rises with the knees; -0.08 cm from the thighs at the closest
kinematics.norm: Resting on the lower thighs just behind the knees, steadied by the hands (common setup; clinical opinion)

kinematics.peak: 1.0 s up, 0.8 s pause, 1.8 s down, 0.6 s reset
kinematics.norm: About 1-2 s up and 2 s down; Kinoshita 2023 trained at 2 s up, 2 s down

cautions: Choose a ball heavy enough to load the calves but easy to hold steady on the thighs.
Rest the ball on the thigh muscle just behind the kneecaps, not on the kneecaps.
Stop if sharp pain, numbness or cramping occurs.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Achilles or plantar heel pain: smaller range and slower tempo.
Knee discomfort under the ball: fold a towel over the thighs.
progressions: Heavier ball, or a dumbbell across each thigh.
Balls of the feet on a plate or step for a deeper stretch.
Single-leg seated raise with the ball on one thigh.

muscleNotes.calves_r: Soleus-biased plantarflexion: with the knee bent 90 degrees the two-joint gastrocnemius is slack. In a 12-week trial seated (knee 90 degrees) calf raises grew the soleus as much as standing raises (2.9% vs 2.1%) but barely changed the gastrocnemius (0.6-1.7% vs 9-12% standing; Kinoshita 2023).
muscleNotes.calves_l: Soleus-biased plantarflexion: with the knee bent 90 degrees the two-joint gastrocnemius is slack. In a 12-week trial seated (knee 90 degrees) calf raises grew the soleus as much as standing raises (2.9% vs 2.1%) but barely changed the gastrocnemius (0.6-1.7% vs 9-12% standing; Kinoshita 2023).
muscleNotes.forearm_flexors_r: The hands press lightly on the sides of the ball to keep it on the thighs.
muscleNotes.forearm_flexors_l: The hands press lightly on the sides of the ball to keep it on the thighs.
muscleNotes.core: Keeps the trunk tall on the bench (clinical opinion).
